claim: The Production front asks for a casual 'Thanks', which is exactly what the earlier card doumo (chapter-5) taught, so a learner will answer どうも as often as ありがとう.
evidence: Production front: 'Thanks. (casual) / casual style'. Earlier card doumo: 'どうも | Thanks.' with note 'A casual, shortened 'thanks' dropped from どうもありがとう'.
fix: Cue the form on the front, e.g. a hint 'ありがとうございます without ございます', or a scene that rules out どうも.
verdictReason: Rendered Production front: 'Greetings / Thanks. (casual) / casual style'. chapter-5/doumo ships (not excluded) as どうも | 'Thanks.' with a note calling it 'a casual, shortened thanks', so どうも satisfies the front exactly. Preflight's collision check passed because the two English strings differ ('Thanks.' vs 'Thanks. (casual)'), so this is not already reported. The card is the book's line and stays; the fix belongs on the hint or a scene (e.g. the book's: a friend says you can come to their party).

claim: The English is nearly the same as the chapter-16 card chotto-decline, where 'Well, it's a bit...' was answered by ちょっと alone, so nothing on this front tells the learner to add えー.
evidence: Production front: 'Well, that's a bit... (casual refusal) / A friend asks to borrow something you'd rather not lend / casual style'. Earlier card chotto-decline: 'ちょっと | Well, it's a bit... (used to decline politely)'.
fix: Add a hint that names the hesitation sound (e.g. 'start with a drawn-out "eh"'), or reword the English so 'Well' is not already owned by bare ちょっと.
verdictReason: Rendered Production front: 'Well, that's a bit... (casual refusal) / A friend asks to borrow something you'd rather not lend / casual style'. Ledger has chapter-16/chotto-decline: ちょっと | 'Well, it's a bit... (used to decline politely)' and chapter-21 すみませんが、ちょっと… | 'Sorry, but...'. Bare ちょっと… is itself the casual (no すみませんが) version, so '(casual refusal)' does not call for えー; nothing on the front does. Book prints えー、ちょっと… in both dialogues 1 and 4, so the target stays; cue the hesitation sound on the front.

claim: Bare いった on the Recognition front can also be read as 'said': the learner knows いう (chapter-19), and this chapter's own extras card casual-request-itte teaches that いって from いう is spelled like いって from いく.
evidence: Recognition front: 'いった' with no scene. Earlier card iu-dict-form: 'いう | Say (dictionary form)'. Extras note: 'いって here is the て-form of いう (iu, "say"), spelled the same as いって from いく (iku, "go")'. The sibling cards ta-kita and ta-shita do carry scenes.
fix: Add a short scene about going somewhere (e.g. 'Talking about where you went last weekend'), as ta-kita and ta-shita have.
verdictReason: Rendered Recognition front: bare いった, no scene. Ledger has chapter-19 いう | 'Say (dictionary form)' and いって | 'Say (て-form)', and this chapter's extras casual-request-itte note says いって (say) is spelled like いって (go); this chapter's own た-form rule (て → た) then yields いった = 'said'. No card anywhere teaches いった as 'said' (grepped every cards.json: only ta-itta and こうえんにいった), so the collision is with a form the learner can derive, which is why polish. ta-kita and ta-shita carry scenes; the same one-line scene settles it.

claim: The note ranks いや as 'stronger than' だめ, a comparison nothing earlier supports and that reads as doubtful, since the だめ card itself calls だめ 'a firm, flat refusal'.
evidence: Note: 'A blunt refusal; the だ (da) is optional. Stronger than だめ (dame), which says something isn't allowed rather than that you don't want to.' Card no-good-dame note: 'A firm, flat refusal.'
fix: Keep the useful distinction (not wanting to vs. not allowed) and drop the 'stronger than' ranking.
verdictReason: Book, Sample Dialogue 1: だめ is 'A firm refusal' ('No.' 'That can't happen.'); Sample Dialogue 4: いや(だ) is used 'when refusing outright' ('I don't want to'). The book ranks neither above the other, and no-good-dame's own note calls だめ 'a firm, flat refusal'. The not-allowed vs. don't-want-to contrast IS the book's and should stay; only the 'Stronger than' ranking is unsourced.

claim: '(male speaker)' fits both male pronouns the learner knows, ぼく and おれ, so ぼくはまだ is as good an answer as おれはまだ.
evidence: Production front: 'I haven't yet. (male speaker) / Asked whether you've read the new manga yet / casual style'. Earlier cards: pronoun-boku 'ぼく | I (casual, used mainly by men).' and pronoun-ore 'おれ | I (casual and rougher, used by men).'
fix: Make the hint pick the pronoun, e.g. '(rough male speaker)' or 'using おれ', and add a note on why は is kept here.
verdictReason: Rendered Production front: 'I haven't yet. (male speaker) / Asked whether you've read the new manga yet / casual style'. Ledger has chapter-25 pronoun-boku ぼく | 'I (casual, used mainly by men)' and pronoun-ore おれ | 'I (casual and rougher, used by men)', so ぼくはまだ fits the hint as well. Same gap this run already confirmed on chapter-25-extras/ore-2 and ore-3 with the same hint wording. The target is the book's line (Abe: おれは まだ), including は, so the fix is the hint; the proposed は note is optional since the book itself keeps it.

claim: The card keeps は after あたし while its near twin from Casual Style 1 drops it, and there is no note to say why, so a learner following the earlier pattern will answer あたし、いかない.
evidence: Production front: 'I'm not going. (female speaker) / casual style', answer 'あたしはいかない', no note. Earlier card ore-2: 'おれ、いかない | I'm not going. (male speaker)'; atashi-gakusei-dayo: 'あたし、がくせいだよ'.
fix: Add a note explaining the は (e.g. contrast: 'I, for my part, am not going'), or a scene that makes the contrast clear.
verdictReason: Target is the book's line (Hayashi: あたしは いかない, contrastive after Raja's うん、いく), so it stays as spelled. Rendered Production front: 'I'm not going. (female speaker) / casual style', no scene, no note. Ledger has chapter-25-extras/ore-2 おれ、いかない | 'I'm not going. (male speaker)', the same English with は dropped, so the front cannot tell the learner to keep は. The sibling baito-aru-kara already uses the scene 'Explaining why you can't go to tomorrow's party'; the matching scene here (others are going, you are not) would ground the は without a grammar note.

claim: The card glosses こんどのどよう as 'this Saturday' where the book, and the deck's own こんど card, say 'next'.
evidence: Book, Sample Dialogue 3: 'こんどの どよう、 うち こない ? ... Hayashi: Why don't you come over to my house next Saturday?' Card english: 'Want to come over to my place this Saturday?' Earlier card chapter-9/kondo-next glosses こんど as 'Next, next time'.
fix: Change the English to 'Want to come over to my place next Saturday?'.
verdictReason: Book, Sample Dialogue 3, twice: 'planning to hold a party at her home next Saturday' and 'Why don't you come over to my house next Saturday?'. Card english: 'Want to come over to my place this Saturday?'. Ledger: chapter-9/kondo-next こんど | 'Next, next time'. One-word English change; target is the book's line and stays.

claim: The English 'Won't you go to the park on Saturday?' reads as a question about the listener's plans rather than the invitation the ない-form + rising intonation makes.
evidence: Book, Sample Dialogue 3: 'Express an invitation by using the ない-form with rising intonation', glossed 'Why don't you come over...?'. Card: どようび、こうえんいかない? = 'Won't you go to the park on Saturday?'. Its sibling casual-invitation-eiga (いっしょにえいがみない?) is glossed 'Want to watch a movie together?'.
fix: Gloss it as an invitation, e.g. 'Want to go to the park on Saturday?', matching casual-invitation-eiga.
verdictReason: 'Won't you go to the park on Saturday?' is not false (it is an English invitation idiom), but it is the only one of the chapter's four invitation glosses not in the 'Want to…?' / 'Why don't you…?' form (casual-invitation-konai, casual-invitation-eiga, kondo-no-doyou-uchi-konai), and the book glosses ない? invitations as 'Why don't you…?'. Read cold it can be taken as 'Aren't you going?'. Authored card, so the gloss is free to change; polish is right, the target stays.

claim: The note says every day of the week shortens the way どようび does, which the book never says; it prints only どよう.
evidence: Book, Sample Dialogue 3: 'こんどの どよう、 うち こない ?' with no comment on the shortening. Card note: 'Casual speech often drops the び (bi) of どようび (doyōbi); the other days shorten the same way.'
fix: Drop 'the other days shorten the same way', or keep the note to どようび → どよう.
verdictReason: Book prints どよう once (Sample Dialogue 3) with no comment on the shortening; nothing in the chapter or the ledger lets the learner check 'the other days shorten the same way'. Not among preflight's note-claim lines for this unit (those are baito, mitemo, karitemo, arigatou). The generalization happens to be accurate casual Japanese (げつよう, きんよう, にちよう), so nothing false is taught, which is why polish and not should-fix; dropping the clause loses only an unsourced aside.
